reviews.title: A Midsummer Night's Dream
reviews.author: Eleanor Fairchild
reviews.excerpt: A transcendent production that redefines the genre entirely — the fairy sequences deploy aerial silk work that transforms the stage into a living dreamscape, while the mechanicals bring genuine wit.

reviews.title: Hamlet
reviews.author: Marcus Chen-Ramirez
reviews.excerpt: A commanding central performance anchors this thoughtful modern staging — the soliloquies are delivered with a conversational intimacy that makes the language feel immediate and urgent.

reviews.title: Macbeth
reviews.author: Priya Vasquez-Okonkwo
reviews.excerpt: Visually stunning with occasional pacing issues in Act III — the lighting design creates an atmosphere of perpetual twilight that perfectly mirrors the moral descent of the protagonists.

reviews.title: Romeo and Juliet
reviews.author: James Thornton-Park
reviews.excerpt: Fresh choreography elevates familiar material — the fight scenes are brutal and kinetic while the balcony sequence is reimagined as a fire escape encounter that grounds the romance.

reviews.title: Othello
reviews.author: Sophia Nakamura-Williams
reviews.excerpt: Solid ensemble work but the leads lack chemistry in the crucial early scenes — Iago steals every moment he occupies, making the manipulation feel almost too easy.

reviews.title: The Tempest
reviews.author: Rafael Johansson-Adeyemi
reviews.excerpt: Ambitious staging undermined by muddled direction — the projection mapping is technically impressive but distracts from the language rather than enhancing it.

reviews.title: Titus Andronicus
reviews.author: Diane Kowalski-Huang
reviews.excerpt: Gratuitous staging adds nothing to the text — the decision to lean into graphic violence without satirical framing makes the production feel exploitative rather than provocative.

reviews.title: The Comedy of Errors
reviews.author: Benjamin Osei-Mensah
reviews.excerpt: A complete misfire on every level — the slapstick timing is off, the doubling gimmick confuses rather than delights, and the musical interludes feel imported from a different production entirely.
